pos: n. (the monastic ceremony of washing the feet of brethren or of the poor, performed weekly in the cloister and solemnly on the Thursday before Easter)
etymology: Latin mandatum, a command, from the first word of the antiphon sung at the rite, Mandatum novum do vobis — a new commandment I give unto you; the English word maundy descends from it.
biblical_def: The mandatum was the foot-washing kept in every Benedictine and Cistercian house: a weekly washing of the brethren's feet by those serving in the kitchen that week, a daily washing of the feet of poor guests by the almoner, and the solemn rite on the Thursday of Holy Week when the abbot washed the feet of the community and of thirteen poor men. The name is the first word of the antiphon, taken from “A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another” (Joh 13:34). The act itself is reported in detail: “he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded” (Joh 13:5). Our Lord then draws the inference and leaves no room for symbolism alone: “If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet” (Joh 13:14), “For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you” (Joh 13:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines maundy Thursday as the Thursday in passion week, from the custom of washing the feet of the poor on that day; and mandate as a command, an order, precept or injunction.
webster_full: MAUNDY THURSDAY, n. The Thursday in passion week, or next before Good Friday; so called from the custom of washing the feet of the poor on that day.
MANDATE, n. A command; an order, precept or injunction; a commission.
LAVE, v.t. To wash; to bathe; a word used chiefly in poetry.
TOWEL, n. A cloth used for wiping the hands and for other purposes.
BASON, n. A hollow vessel or dish, to hold water for washing, and for various other uses.
scriptures: Joh 13:5
After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded.
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.
corruption_summary: The weekly washing of feet in the cloister, named from the commandment sung over it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the rite performed by the great upon the poor once a year with a towel they do not need to use again — the royal maundy and its monastic equivalent, where an abbot washed thirteen already-clean feet before an audience. The ceremony survived the thing it signified. Our Lord's own action is pointedly undignified and unobserved by any public, and the command attached to it is “ye also ought to wash one another's feet” (Joh 13:14) — one another, not the deserving poor on a stage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an example is given to be copied in substance and not only in form. Whether a congregation keeps a literal foot-washing is a matter on which Reformed churches have differed without heat; what is not optional is the humility of taking the lowest service for a brother, which is what “that ye should do as I have done to you” (Joh 13:15) requires of everyone who has read it.
roots_summary: Latin mandatum novum, a new commandment; Greek entole (G1785), a commandment; Greek nipto (G3538), to wash a part of the body; Greek hupodeigma (G5262), an example; Greek lention (G3012), a linen towel.
roots_lines: Latin mandatum — a command, the antiphon's first word; English maundy.
Greek entole (G1785) — a commandment; “A new commandment I give unto you” (Joh 13:34).
Greek nipto (G3538) — to wash the hands or feet; “have washed your feet” (Joh 13:14).
Greek lention (G3012) — a linen cloth, a towel; “the towel wherewith he was girded” (Joh 13:5).
Greek hupodeigma (G5262) — a pattern, an example; “For I have given you an example” (Joh 13:15).
usage: “he poureth water into a bason” (Joh 13:5) — the act the rite is named from.
“If I then, your Lord and Master” (Joh 13:14) — the argument from the greater.
“as I have loved you” (Joh 13:34) — the measure of the new commandment.

pos: n. (a monk or canon holding one of the offices of a monastery under the abbot — cellarer, sacrist, almoner, kitchener and the rest)
etymology: Medieval Latin obedientiarius, from obedientia, obedience; an office was an obedientia, a charge received by obedience rather than sought.
biblical_def: An obedientiary was a monk who held one of the working offices of a house: the cellarer who bought and stored, the sacrist who kept the church and its vessels, the almoner who distributed to the poor, the kitchener, the infirmarer, the hosteller, the precentor over the singing. The name is exact and is the whole theory of the system: an office was an obedientia, a charge laid on a man by his superior, not a post he applied for, and each officer rendered account at the annual audit. Most houses that fell apart fell apart here, in the accounts. Scripture sets the standard for the whole class of men in one sentence: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). Not successful, not gifted — found faithful, which implies an examiner. Our Lord's parable supplies the audit: “give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward” (Luk 16:2). And Peter extends the office to every Christian: “As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1Pe 4:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obedience as compliance with a command, prohibition or known law and rule of duty; and steward as a man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns and keep the accounts.
webster_full: OBEDIENCE, n. Compliance with a command, prohibition, or known law and rule of duty prescribed; the performance of what is required or enjoined by authority.
STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, collect the rents or income, keep the accounts.
OFFICE, n. A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose; an employment undertaken by commission or authority.
AUDIT, n. An examination of an account or of accounts, with a hearing of the parties concerned, by proper officers.
CELLARER, n. An officer in a monastery who has the care of the cellar, or the charge of procuring and keeping the provisions.
scriptures: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Luk 16:2
And he called him, and said unto him, How is it that I hear this of thee? give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward.
As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.
Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.
corruption_summary: The monk who held an office by obedience rather than ambition, and rendered account for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the office sought, and then kept. The later medieval houses are full of obedientiaries who treated a charge as a freehold, farmed its revenues, and resisted the audit; the visitation records are a catalogue of it. The remedy in the rule was the annual account, and the remedy in Scripture is the same with a different auditor: “How is it that I hear this of thee?” (Luk 16:2) is a question from a master who has been told something.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the identity Paul claims before he states the requirement: “Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1Co 4:1). A steward owns nothing and originates nothing; he distributes what was entrusted. That is as true of a preacher with a pulpit as of a cellarer with a granary, and it is why faithfulness and not fruitfulness is the thing required.
roots_summary: Latin obedientiarius, an office-holder; Greek oikonomos (G3623), a steward; Greek oikonomia (G3622), stewardship; Greek pistos (G4103), faithful; Greek huperetes (G5257), an under-rower or servant.
roots_lines: Latin obedientia — obedience; an office received, not sought.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a house manager, a steward; “stewards of the mysteries of God” (1Co 4:1).
Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy; “that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).
Greek oikonomia (G3622) — administration, stewardship; “give an account of thy stewardship” (Luk 16:2).
Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; “As every man hath received the gift” (1Pe 4:10).
usage: “it is required in stewards” (1Co 4:2) — the requirement, and it is one thing.
“thou mayest be no longer steward” (Luk 16:2) — the end of an unaudited office.
“as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1Pe 4:10) — every believer an obedientiary.

pos: n. (the building beside a monastery gate where alms were given out, and where the almoner kept his stores)
etymology: Old French aumosnerie, from Latin eleemosyna, alms, from Greek eleemosune, mercy or pity shown in giving.
biblical_def: The almonry stood at or near the gate of a monastery, outside the cloister proper, and from it the almoner distributed the broken meats from the refectory, clothing, and in some houses schooling for almonry boys. The arrangement was deliberate: the poor were received at the gate, not in the choir, and the office existed so that charity was a scheduled duty rather than a mood. The word is Greek before it is English, and the Greek is the word for mercy. The Lord's teaching on it is almost entirely about concealment: “when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men” (Mat 6:2), followed by the standard that has governed Christian giving ever since: “when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Mat 6:3). The promise attached is not that the gift goes unnoticed but that it is noticed by the right person: “thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly” (Mat 6:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines almonry as the place where the almoner resides, or where alms are distributed; and alms as any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor.
webster_full: ALMONRY, n. The place where the almoner resides, or where the alms are distributed.
ALMS, n. Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing; a charitable gift.
ALMONER, n. An officer whose duty is to distribute charity or alms.
CHARITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will. Liberality to the poor, consisting in almsgiving or benefactions.
HYPOCRITE, n. One who feigns to be what he is not; one who has the form of godliness without the power.
scriptures: Mat 6:2

Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Mat 6:3
But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:
Mat 6:4
That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.
Act 9:36
Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.
corruption_summary: The building at the gate where the broken meats were given out, and the commandment that giving be hidden.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is alms as display, which our Lord names before he names anything else about giving, and which an institution finds almost impossible to avoid: a great house with an almonry at its gate is visibly charitable, and the visibility is itself the reward. “Verily I say unto you, They have their reward” (Mat 6:2) is a closed account. The trumpet need not be literal; a plaque, an annual report or a named wing will serve.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that giving is a commanded and ordinary duty, not an occasional heroism — the Lord says when thou doest alms, not if. The woman at Joppa is the pattern and the record of her is a list of garments: “this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did” (Act 9:36). Nothing in the account suggests she was conscious of being an example.
roots_summary: Greek eleemosune (G1654), alms or mercy shown; Greek eleos (G1656), mercy; Greek hupokrites (G5273), an actor or hypocrite; Greek misthos (G3408), wages or reward; Greek kruptos (G2927), secret.
roots_lines: Greek eleemosune (G1654) — mercy shown in giving, whence alms and almonry.
Greek hupokrites (G5273) — a stage actor, a pretender; “as the hypocrites do in the synagogues” (Mat 6:2).
Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, reward; “They have their reward” (Mat 6:2).
Greek kruptos (G2927) — hidden, secret; “That thine alms may be in secret” (Mat 6:4).
Greek agathos (G18) — good, beneficent; “full of good works and almsdeeds” (Act 9:36).
usage: “do not sound a trumpet before thee” (Mat 6:2) — the first rule of the almonry.
“let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Mat 6:3) — the standard, impossibly high.
“himself shall reward thee openly” (Mat 6:4) — the reward relocated, not removed.

pos: n. (the building in a monastery set apart for the sick and the aged, with its own hall, chapel and kitchen)
etymology: Medieval Latin infirmaria, from infirmus, not firm, weak — the house of the weak.
biblical_def: The infirmary was a separate range within the monastic precinct, with its own hall, chapel, kitchen and often its own garden of herbs, where the sick, the very old and those recovering from the regular bloodletting were housed under a relaxed rule — meat was allowed there when it was allowed nowhere else. It is the most attractive institution the monasteries produced, and it is the direct ancestor of the hospital. Its warrant is unambiguous. The King in the judgement scene names it among the deeds done to himself: “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36). James gives the congregation a procedure rather than a sentiment: “Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (Jam 5:14). And the definition of undefiled religion is a visit to the people least able to repay it: “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infirmary as a lodging or apartment for the sick, a hospital; and infirmity as an unsound or unhealthy state of the body, weakness, feebleness.
webster_full: INFIRMARY, n. A lodging or apartment for the sick; a hospital or place where the sick and infirm are received and treated.
INFIRMITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness. A failing; a fault; foible.
HOSPITAL, n. A building appropriated for the reception of sick, infirm and helpless paupers, who are supported and nursed by charity.
VISIT, v.t. To go or come to see; to attend. To go or come to see for the purpose of comforting or relieving.
ANOINT, v.t. To pour oil upon; to smear or rub over with oil or unctuous substances.
scriptures: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
Jam 5:14
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
corruption_summary: The monastic sick-house with its relaxed rule, ancestor of the hospital, and the King who counts a visit as made to himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the care of the sick detached from the church and handed wholly to a profession, so that the congregation's duty is discharged by taxation and the elders are not called. James assumes that the sick man's first call is to the elders, and the modern believer's first call is to a clinic. The clinic is a mercy and should be used; the elders are a command and are usually not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the identification the King makes, which is the strongest motive Scripture gives for any work of mercy: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40). The monastic infirmarer was taught to see Christ in the man in the bed, and if that is read as a figure it is too weak; the text says it plainly.
roots_summary: Latin infirmus, weak; Greek astheneo (G770), to be weak or sick; Greek episkeptomai (G1980), to visit or look after; Greek presbuteros (G4245), an elder; Greek aleipho (G218), to anoint.
roots_lines: Latin infirmaria — from infirmus, not firm, weak.
Greek astheneo (G770) — to be feeble, to be sick; “Is any sick among you?” (Jam 5:14).
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to look upon, to visit with care; “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36).
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — an elder; “let him call for the elders of the church” (Jam 5:14).
Greek aleipho (G218) — to anoint with oil; “anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (Jam 5:14).
usage: “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36) — the charter of every infirmary.
“let them pray over him” (Jam 5:14) — the call that is usually not made.
“Pure religion and undefiled before God” (Jam 1:27) — defined as a visit.

pos: n. (the monastic officer in charge of the kitchen, the cooking rota and the serving of the community's meals)
etymology: Medieval Latin coquinarius, from coquina, a kitchen, from coquere, to cook — the officer of the kitchen.
biblical_def: The kitchener ordered the food, kept the kitchen accounts, and set the weekly rota by which every monk in turn served his brethren at table — in the Benedictine rule no one was exempt but the sick and those occupied in weightier business, and the week ended with the outgoing servers washing the feet of the community. It is the office that most nearly reproduces an apostolic arrangement. When the Hellenist widows were neglected, the twelve did not abolish the work but refused to let it displace their own: “It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables” (Act 6:2), and so they ordered the church to “look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business” (Act 6:3). The qualifications are striking for a job about food. Martha's kitchen supplies the other half of the lesson, which is that serving can crowd out the one thing needful: “Martha was cumbered about much serving” (Luk 10:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines kitchen as a cook room, the room of a house appropriated to cookery; and serve as to work for, to attend at command, to wait on.
webster_full: KITCHEN, n. A cook room; the room of a house appropriated to cookery.
SERVE, v.t. To work for; to bestow the labor of body and mind in the employment of another. To attend at command; to wait on.
COOK, n. One whose occupation is to prepare victuals for the table; a man or woman who dresses provisions.
CUMBER, v.t. To check, stop or retard, as motion; to make motion difficult; to obstruct; to perplex or embarrass.
PROVISION, n. The act of providing or making previous preparation. Things provided; preparation; measures taken beforehand. Stores provided; food; victuals.
scriptures: Act 6:2
Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples unto them, and said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.
Act 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
But Martha was cumbered about much serving, and came to him, and said, Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me.
But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
corruption_summary: The officer over the kitchen and the weekly serving rota, and the apostles who would not let tables displace the word.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs in two directions and the church has gone wrong both ways. The first is the ministry swallowed by administration, which is what the twelve refused; a preacher consumed by the practical has not become humbler, he has abandoned a post. The second is the contempt for the practical, which the apostles equally refused, since they required of table-servers that they be “full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ's gentle correction of a woman who was not doing anything wrong. “But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luk 10:42) does not condemn the cooking; it refuses to let the cook set the agenda for the house. The monastic rota, which put every monk in the kitchen for a week and then took him out again, understood this better than most parishes do.
roots_summary: Latin coquina, a kitchen; Greek diakoneo (G1247), to serve; Greek trapeza (G5132), a table; Greek perispao (G4049), to be distracted; Greek chreia (G5532), need.
roots_lines: Latin coquinarius — the officer of the coquina or kitchen.
Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve, to minister; “and serve tables” (Act 6:2).
Greek trapeza (G5132) — a table; the word behind the apostles' phrase.
Greek sophia (G4678) — wisdom; “full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3).
Greek perispao (G4049) — to be drawn about, distracted; “Martha was cumbered about much serving” (Luk 10:40).
usage: “It is not reason that we should leave the word of God” (Act 6:2) — the refusal that is not pride.
“men of honest report” (Act 6:3) — the qualifications for a kitchen office.
“But one thing is needful” (Luk 10:42) — said in a kitchen, kindly.

pos: n. (the monastic officer in charge of the refectory — its linen, cups, benches, reading desk and the order of the common meal)
etymology: Medieval Latin refectorarius, from refectorium, a place of refreshment, from reficere, to restore or remake.
biblical_def: The refectorian kept the frater: he laid the tables, washed the cloths and cups, saw that the reading desk was ready and the lamp lit, and governed the order in which the community came in, sat, and left. The room he kept was the second most important in a monastery after the church, because the rule understood a meal eaten together in silence under the reading of Scripture to be an act of the common life rather than a pause from it. The apostolic church ate the same way: “continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart” (Act 2:46). Paul had to legislate for a congregation where the meal had gone wrong, and his correction is exactly a refectorian's concern with order: “when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another” (1Co 11:33), because at Corinth “every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken” (1Co 11:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refectory as a room of refreshment, properly a hall in convents where a moderate repast is taken; and repast as the act of taking food, the food taken, a meal.
webster_full: REFECTORY, n. A room of refreshment; properly, a hall or apartment in convents and monasteries, where a moderate repast is taken.
REPAST, n. The act of taking food. That which is taken; food; victuals; a meal.
FRATER, n. In monastic use, the refectory or common dining hall of a religious house.
TARRY, v.i. To stay; to abide; to continue; to lodge. To wait; to attend.
DECENCY, n. Propriety of form in social intercourse, in words or in actions; opposed to indecorum.
scriptures: Act 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
Wherefore, my brethren, when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another.
For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: The officer who kept the common table in order, and the Corinthian supper that had lost it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the common meal that stops being common. At Corinth the mechanism was the arrival time and the private basket: those who could come early ate their own food in front of those who could not, and Paul calls the result a thing that cannot be called the Lord's supper at all. The social division did the damage, and it did it at a table meant to display the opposite.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that order in the assembly is a spiritual matter and not fussiness: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) closes a chapter about the Spirit's gifts, not about furniture. A refectorian washing cups and setting benches so that a hundred men can eat together without confusion is doing the work that verse describes, and the gladness of “singleness of heart” (Act 2:46) is what such order exists to protect.
roots_summary: Latin reficere, to restore; Greek klasis artou, breaking of bread; Greek ekdechomai (G1551), to wait for; Greek aphelotes (G858), singleness or simplicity; Greek taxis (G5010), order.
roots_lines: Latin refectorium — a place of restoring, from reficere, to remake.
Greek aphelotes (G858) — simplicity, singleness; “with gladness and singleness of heart” (Act 2:46).
Greek ekdechomai (G1551) — to wait for, to expect; “tarry one for another” (1Co 11:33).
Greek prolambano (G4301) — to take beforehand; “every one taketh before other his own supper” (1Co 11:21).
Greek taxis (G5010) — arrangement, order; “decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
usage: “breaking bread from house to house” (Act 2:46) — the first refectory.
“one is hungry, and another is drunken” (1Co 11:21) — what disorder at table means.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the refectorian's verse.

pos: n. (the monastic officer charged with receiving guests — also spelt hostiller or hostillar; keeper of the guest house)
etymology: Old French hostelier, from hostel, a lodging, from Latin hospitale, a place for guests, from hospes, a guest or host.
biblical_def: The hosteller kept the guest house, received travellers at the gate, assigned beds, found fodder for horses, and was instructed by the rule to meet every arrival as he would meet Christ. Great houses on pilgrim roads received hundreds a year, from bishops to beggars, and the office was one of the most expensive in the monastery and the most abused by guests. Its warrant is a command, not a courtesy: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2) — an allusion to Abraham at Mamre, where the hospitality came first and the identification of the guests came after. Peter adds the hard clause that separates hospitality from entertaining: “Use hospitality one to another without grudging” (1Pe 4:9), and Paul makes it a standing habit of the whole church: “Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13). It is also a qualification for the eldership, which means a man unwilling to open his house is unqualified to lead one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, with kindness and without grudging; and hostler as the person who has the care of horses at an inn.
webster_full: HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
HOSTLER, n. The person who has the care of horses at an inn.
GUEST, n. A stranger or visitor entertained gratuitously, either at the house or table of another.
GRUDGE, v.t. To envy one the possession of; to give or take unwillingly, with reluctance.
ENTERTAIN, v.t. To receive into the house and treat with hospitality, either at the table only, or with lodging also.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
corruption_summary: The officer who met every traveller as he would meet Christ, and the command that hospitality be given without grudging.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is hospitality turned into an industry, which happened to the monasteries along the pilgrim roads: the guest house became an inn, the offerings became a tariff, and the stranger became a customer. The slide is natural and almost invisible, and Peter's clause is placed exactly where it catches it. A host who keeps accounts of what his hospitality has cost him is already grudging; “without grudging” (1Pe 4:9) forbids the ledger as well as the complaint.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that hospitality is a qualification for office and therefore a normal Christian duty, not a gift some have. “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2) puts it in a list with sobriety and teaching. The promise in Hebrews is not a reason to do it, but it is a warning about who may be at the door.
roots_summary: Latin hospes, a guest or host; Greek philoxenia (G5381), love of strangers; Greek xenos (G3581), a stranger; Greek goggusmos (G1112), murmuring; Greek philoxenos (G5382), hospitable.
roots_lines: Latin hospitale — a place for guests, from hospes, guest or host.
Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers, hospitality; “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2).
Greek xenizo (G3579) — to receive as a guest; “some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).
Greek goggusmos (G1112) — grumbling, murmuring; “without grudging” (1Pe 4:9).
Greek philoxenos (G5382) — hospitable, fond of guests; “given to hospitality” (1Ti 3:2).
usage: “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2) — a warning about the door.
“Use hospitality one to another” (1Pe 4:9) — mutual, not one-directional.
“given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13) — a settled habit of the church.

pos: n. (a right of maintenance in a monastery — board, lodging and a stipend for life — granted to a patron, sold for cash, or imposed by a king on a house)
etymology: Medieval Latin corrodium, from corrodere in the sense of consuming together; an allowance of provisions taken from a house.
biblical_def: A corrody was a life interest in a monastery's hospitality: so many loaves and gallons of ale a week, a chamber, a servant, firewood, and sometimes a money fee. Founders' families claimed them by right, kings imposed them on houses to pension off retired servants, and poor houses sold them outright for ready cash — a medieval annuity, and like all annuities it tended to be sold cheap by a seller in trouble and to last longer than expected. Corrodies ruined several English abbeys. The arrangement has one luminous biblical counterpart and one warning. The counterpart is Mephibosheth: “I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually” (2Sa 9:7), a place at the king's table given for another man's sake to a man with nothing to offer. The warning is the seller's: a house that sold its future bread for present money had done what Esau did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines corody as an allowance of meat, drink and clothing due to the king from an abbey or religious house; and annuity as a sum of money payable yearly to continue for a given number of years, or for life.
webster_full: CORODY, n. An allowance of meat, drink or clothing, due to the king from an abbey or other religious house, for the sustenance of such of his servants as he may think proper to bestow it on.
ANNUITY, n. A sum of money payable yearly, to continue for a given number of years, for life, or forever.
MAINTENANCE, n. Sustenance; sustentation; support by means of supplies of food, clothing and other conveniences.
PENSION, n. An annual allowance of a sum of money to a person by government, for past services.
STIPEND, n. Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily, monthly or annual.
scriptures: And David said unto him, Fear not: for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually.
So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem: for he did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet.
And Jacob said, Swear to me this day; and he sware unto him: and he sold his birthright unto Jacob.
Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
corruption_summary: A life pension of bread and ale charged on a monastery, sold cheap by houses in trouble.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sale of tomorrow's bread for today's money, which is the whole history of the corrody. A house short of cash sold a corrody for a lump sum and then fed the holder for thirty years. Scripture has the archetype and does not soften it: Esau “sold his birthright unto Jacob” (Gen 25:33) for a meal, and Hebrews calls him “profane person, as Esau” (Heb 12:16) for it — profane meaning that he treated a holy thing as ordinary merchandise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the opposite transaction, where a place at the table is given and not bought. Mephibosheth is lame, landless and the grandson of the king's enemy, and the ground of his pension is named: “for Jonathan thy father's sake” (2Sa 9:7). So “he did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet” (2Sa 9:13) — the two facts set side by side, which is the gospel in a sentence.
roots_summary: Latin corrodium, an allowance of provisions; Hebrew chesed (H2617), covenant kindness; Hebrew lechem (H3899), bread; Hebrew bekorah (H1062), a birthright; Greek bebelos (G952), profane.
roots_lines: Latin corrodium — an allowance of food and lodging charged on a house.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant kindness; “I will surely shew thee kindness” (2Sa 9:7).
Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread, food; “thou shalt eat bread at my table continually” (2Sa 9:7).
Hebrew bekorah (H1062) — a birthright; “sold his birthright unto Jacob” (Gen 25:33).
Greek bebelos (G952) — profane, treating holy things as common; “profane person, as Esau” (Heb 12:16).
usage: “for Jonathan thy father's sake” (2Sa 9:7) — the ground of an undeserved pension.
“and was lame on both his feet” (2Sa 9:13) — the fact the table did not remove.
“for one morsel of meat sold his birthright” (Heb 12:16) — the seller's side of a corrody.

pos: n. (originally an extra portion of food or drink served in a monastery on a feast day or from a benefactor's bequest; now a trifling allowance)
etymology: Old French pitance, from Latin pietas, piety or dutiful kindness — a portion given out of piety, which came to mean a portion barely worth giving.
biblical_def: A pittance was the small extra that relieved the monastic diet: an egg, a dish of fish, a measure of wine, served on a saint's day or paid for out of a benefactor's legacy, with the donor's name read out. Houses kept pittance accounts and pittancers to administer them. The word's descent is one of the sharpest in English: from pietas, dutiful love, to a sum so small it is an insult. That descent is itself the entry. Agur's prayer asks for neither extreme and names the danger in each: “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me” (Pro 30:8) — convenient meaning allotted, the portion that fits. Our Lord taught his disciples to ask for exactly that and no more: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Mat 6:11). The petition is for a day at a time, and a man who has prayed it cannot sneer at a small portion, because small and sufficient are not the same word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pittance as an allowance of meat in a monastery, and hence a very small portion allowed or assigned; and competence as property or means of subsistence sufficient to furnish the necessaries and conveniences of life.
webster_full: PITTANCE, n. An allowance of meat in a monastery. A very small portion allowed or assigned. A very small quantity.
COMPETENCE, n. Property or means of subsistence sufficient to furnish the necessaries and conveniences of life, without superfluity.
ALLOWANCE, n. The act of allowing or admitting. A stated quantity, as of food or drink; hence, abatement; deduction.
SUFFICIENT, a. Enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; competent.
CONVENIENT, a. Fit; suitable; proper; adapted to use or to wants. In Scripture, that which is needful or allotted.
scriptures: Pro 30:8
Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me:
Pro 30:9
Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.
Mat 6:11
Give us this day our daily bread.
And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
corruption_summary: The extra dish served in a cloister out of piety, and the word's long fall into an insult.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is in the word itself and in what the word records. A portion given out of pietas became a byword for a sum too small to live on, because the givers kept the name and shrank the gift. Agur anticipated the spiritual arithmetic on both sides: riches tempt a man to say “Who is the LORD?” (Pro 30:9), and poverty tempts him to steal and “take the name of my God in vain” (Pro 30:9). Neither is romanticised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the definition of enough, which Scripture sets startlingly low and never apologises for: “And having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8). That is not a counsel for the poor only; it is the apostolic standard for everyone, and it is the sentence that makes the daily-bread petition prayable in earnest rather than as a formality by people with a full larder.
roots_summary: Latin pietas, dutiful kindness; Hebrew choq (H2706), an appointed portion; Greek epiousios (G1967), sufficient for the day; Greek autarkes (G842), self-sufficient or content; Hebrew taraph (H2963), to provide food.
roots_lines: Latin pietas — dutiful love; whence pitance, a portion given out of piety.
Hebrew choq (H2706) — an appointed portion, an allotted due; “feed me with food convenient for me” (Pro 30:8).
Greek epiousios (G1967) — for the coming day, sufficient; “Give us this day our daily bread” (Mat 6:11).
Greek arkeo (G714) — to be enough, to suffice; “let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8).
Hebrew resh (H7389) — poverty; “give me neither poverty nor riches” (Pro 30:8).
usage: “food convenient for me” (Pro 30:8) — the portion that fits, not the portion that impresses.
“Give us this day” (Mat 6:11) — a day at a time, which is how a pittance comes.
“having food and raiment” (1Ti 6:8) — the apostolic definition of enough.

pos: n. (a lay brotherhood attached to a monastery or parish, whose members were admitted to a share in the house's prayers and merits in return for gifts or dues)
etymology: Medieval Latin confraternitas, from con, together, and frater, a brother — a company of those made brothers.
biblical_def: A confraternity was a body of lay men and women formally associated with a religious house or a parish. Members paid dues or gave land, were enrolled in a register read out in chapter, buried their dead with the community's prayers, kept a feast, and above all were admitted to a share in the merits of the house — a participation in the spiritual benefit of prayers they did not say. The social good was real: the confraternities ran lights, relieved widows, buried the poor and became the guilds. The theology is the problem, and it is exactly the point at which a true doctrine was inverted. The New Testament knows a genuine fellowship and names its content: “And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42). It is a fellowship of participants, not of subscribers, and the thing shared is doctrine, bread and prayer, none of which can be purchased or assigned.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confraternity as a brotherhood, a society or body of men united for some purpose or in some profession; and fellowship as companionship, society, consort, mutual association on equal and friendly terms.
webster_full: CONFRATERNITY, n. A brotherhood; a society or body of men united for some purpose or in some profession.
FELLOWSHIP, n. Companionship; society; consort; mutual association of persons on equal and friendly terms; familiar intercourse.
GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or company, associated for some purpose, particularly for carrying on commerce.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward.
ENROLL, v.t. To write in a roll or register; to insert a name in a catalogue.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us: and truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ.
But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: A lay brotherhood bought into a monastery's prayers, and the fellowship that cannot be subscribed to.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the transferable merit, which is the hinge of the whole system: if a house has a surplus of prayer and holiness, shares in it may be sold, and the confraternity register is the shareholders' list. Scripture allows no such transfer. John grounds fellowship in a shared relation to persons, not in an assignment of benefit: “truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1Jo 1:3). There is no surplus to sell because there was never a stock.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fellowship is a consequence of walking in the light and is tested by it: “But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin” (1Jo 1:7). The modern substitute for the confraternity is the membership that confers belonging without presence, and the plain answer to it remains “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).
roots_summary: Latin confraternitas, a brotherhood; Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship or participation; Greek adelphotes (G81), brotherhood; Greek episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together; Greek metecho (G3348), to partake.
roots_lines: Latin con + frater — those made brothers together.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, participation; “in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42).
Greek adelphotes (G81) — the brotherhood, the body of brethren.
Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together; “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25).
Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse; “cleanseth us from all sin” (1Jo 1:7).
usage: “And they continued stedfastly” (Act 2:42) — the mark of real fellowship.
“our fellowship is with the Father” (1Jo 1:3) — the ground, which cannot be assigned.
“as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25) — membership without presence, named in the first century.
